newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU presses for OAU force for Zaire crisis.
newsitem.headline: EU presses for OAU force for Zaire crisis.

text.p: The European Union wants the Organisation of African Unity to send troops to guarantee the safety of a million refugees fleeing fighting in Zaire, an Irish government minister said on Wednesday.
"There should be a force to monitor and protect refugees. This should be from the OAU with logistical support from the EU," said Joan Burton, minister of state for overseas aid.

Burton, whose country currently holds the EU presidency, said she hoped an outline agreement on this as well as a ceasefire between all parties in the area would be agreed at a planned regional summit in coming days.
It was believed to be the first time the 15-member EU had publicly proposed that the 54-nation OAU assemble its own peace-keeping force to protect refugees at risk.

The last major foreign force despatched to a conflict in Africa was a U.S.-led multinational army sent to police the distribution of famine aid to Somalia in the early 1990s until it was withdrawn in 1994 after coming under guerrilla attack.
The OAU has had a chequered history in assembling peace forces in the recent past, but is keen to be seen as the continent's policeman, ending reliance on foreign forces.
Burton was speaking after talks with Rwandan Foreign Minister Anastase Gasana as his government and Zaire moved closer to war after trading artillery fire across their border for several days.
She said she hoped the talks would produce a ceasefire in a conflict which flared when ethnic Tutsis in eastern Zaire said they were being expelled by Zairean government troops.
An OAU force would then police corridors down which refugees fleeing the fighting could be taken to safety, she said.
The refugees in Zaire are Rwandan Hutus blamed for the 1994 genocide of Tutsis. They are resisting appeals from the United Nations to return to Rwanda, saying they fear for their lives.

The OAU said it had sent a delegation to Zaire and Rwanda to try to defuse the crisis, and its Conflict Resolution committee would meet on Thursday at its headquarters in Addis Ababa to try to propose solutions.
French President Jacques Chirac urged heads of east and central African states to call a conference quickly over the rapidly deteriorating situation in the region.

"The worsening situation and unacceptable tragedies taking place impose the holding of a conference under the auspices of the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity," government spokesman Alain Lamassoure quoted Chirac as telling the weekly French cabinet meeting.
